source: The parameter list of each function's prototype as Microsoft documents it in the Win32 API reference and declares it in the Windows SDK headers (synchapi.h, fileapi.h, winbase.h, wininet.h, winhttp.h, urlmon.h), and the documented values of the constants named here (fileapi.h: CREATE_NEW = 1, CREATE_ALWAYS = 2). The Windows ABI fixes each parameter's position; positions are counted from 1. Written for this project, not copied from a third-party table.
about: Which argument of a Windows API function is a whole value of an indicator role, and the text encoding the function reads it in (an A function reads single-byte text, a W function UTF-16LE). A file path is listed only where the call makes or replaces the file it names, or removes it: the destination of a copy or a move, the file a download writes, the file a delete removes, and the file CreateFile opens only when the call's creation disposition is a constant that creates a file (the 'when' condition: that argument's value, read at the call, must be one of 'values'). A path the call only reads or opens as it exists (a copy's source, CreateFile opening an existing file, an attribute change) is left out: such a path is as often the system's own file as the sample's. A registry function's key argument is left out: it names a key under a root handle, not a whole key. A URL argument is left out: a URL the file hides is published by the network rule already.

mutex_name.words: the name of the mutex the call creates or opens

file_path.words: the path of a file the call creates, writes or removes

user_agent.words: the user agent the HTTP session the call opens sends

browser_user_agents.source: The product token the common desktop and mobile browsers begin their User-Agent header with, as the header's grammar places it first (RFC 9110, section 10.1.5): every current browser sends 'Mozilla/5.0 (', an Internet Explorer era one 'Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE ', and the older Presto-based browsers 'Opera/'.
browser_user_agents.about: A bound user agent that begins with one of these, and whose every product and comment token is one the common browsers send (the vocabulary below), keeps its row and its chain but is not published: an indicator for it would match the ordinary browser traffic that sends the same header. One that begins so but carries a product or comment token outside the vocabulary is not a browser's own header, and is published with that token named. A well-known crawler's own token (its name, alone or with its version), with an info URL at that crawler's own domain right after it, is not such a token: an indicator on it would match that crawler's traffic. One that cannot be read as the header's grammar (an unclosed or nested comment, a character no token takes) is left unpublished, as before. A known false negative, kept on purpose: the entries of a comment after its 'Android' entry name the device (a model, a build), which no vocabulary can list, so a token placed there is read past and the value stays unpublished. A second known false negative: a bare two-letter word that is an ISO 639-1 language code is read as an older browser's locale, since refusing it would publish real browsers' headers.

tokens.source: The product names and comment words the mainstream browsers, their engines, in-app and embedded browsers and the platforms they run on place in their own User-Agent header (RFC 9110, section 10.1.5: product *( RWS ( product / comment ) )), with the Internet Explorer era's runtime, toolbar and OEM words its header carried. A version is not a word: a product's '/version', a comment word of digits, dots and underscores or a build ('15E148'), a version after a word's '/' or ':' ('rv:121.0', 'Trident/7.0'), a version run onto a word ('InfoPath.2', 'GTB7.5') and a locale ('en-US', or a bare ISO 639-1 language code from 'languages') are read past. A version is digits, dots and underscores, or a build of digits, one capital letter and digits; a version after '/' or ':' is a digit followed by digits, dots, underscores and hyphens. 'products_beside' lists a product a browser sends only beside one of its own ('Core' beside 'QQBrowser'), and 'comment_words_after' a comment word sent only right after another ('One' after 'Xbox'); 'NP06' to 'NP09' are the OEM words Internet Explorer's comment carried after its platform and 'Trident' entries. 'crawlers' are the well-known crawlers' own names, each with the domains its info URL is at.
